questions.question: What does it mean for a subset $\boldsymbol{E}$ of a space $\boldsymbol{X}$ to be compact?
options: Every finite cover of $\boldsymbol{E}$ has an open subcover.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ has no open covers.
Every open cover of $\boldsymbol{E}$ has a finite subcover.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is always the whole space $\boldsymbol{X}$.

questions.question: Which prerequisite notion appears directly for compactness?
options: Complex conjugate
Open cover
Cauchy sequence only
Boundary point only

questions.question: Which set is compact?
options: $\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:y = x^2\}$
$\mathbb{R}^n$
An arbitrary unbounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$
$\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\|x\|\ \leq 1\}$

questions.question: Which kind of set is compact in every metric space?
options: Any unbounded set
Any finite set
Any non-closed set
Any open cover

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}^n$, which condition is equivalent to compactness for $\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$?
options: $\boldsymbol{E}$ is open and unbounded.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is finite and empty.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is closed and bounded.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ has no open cover.

questions.question: What does 'continuity preserves compactness' mean?
options: If $\boldsymbol{f}$ is compact, then $\boldsymbol{X}$ is continuous.
If $\boldsymbol{f}$ is continuous on compact $\boldsymbol{X}$, then $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{X})$ is compact.
Every image of every set is compact.
Continuity turns every unbounded set into a finite set.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be closed and bounded. What follows?
options: $\boldsymbol{E}$ is not compact.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ has no finite subcover for any open cover.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is compact.
$\boldsymbol{E}$ is not a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

questions.question: If $\boldsymbol{X}\subseteq\boldsymbol{E}$ is compact and $\boldsymbol{f}:\boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}^k$ is continuous on $\boldsymbol{X}$, what can be concluded?
options: $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{X})$ is always empty.
$\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{X})$ cannot be bounded.
$\boldsymbol{X}$ stops being compact.
$\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{X})$ is compact.

questions.question: Which hidden assumption is needed before using “closed and bounded implies compact”?
options: The set is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The set is a subset of $\mathbb{C}$ only.
The set has no open covers.
The set is the image of a discontinuous function.

questions.question: Why does compactness involve “every open cover” rather than one conveniently chosen cover?
options: One finite cover is enough to prove every set compact.
The finite-subcover property must hold for any open cover.
Only covers by one open set are relevant.
Open covers are not part of the definition.

questions.question: An open cover of a finite set $\{p_1,p_2,p_3\}$ is given. Why must it have a finite subcover?
options: Choose infinitely many open sets for each point.
Choose one open set covering each point $p_i$; at most three sets are needed.
No open set can contain any $p_i$.
The cover must be discarded because finite sets are never compact.

questions.question: Let $\boldsymbol{X} = \{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\|x\|\ \leq 1\}$ and let $\boldsymbol{f}$ be continuous on $\boldsymbol{X}$. Which conclusion follows?
options: $\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{X})$ is never compact.
$\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{X})$ is compact.
$\boldsymbol{X}$ is not compact because it is closed.
$\boldsymbol{X}$ is not compact because it is bounded.

questions.question: What is a finite subcover of an open cover of $E$?
options: A cover of finitely many points outside $E$.
A finite set contained in every open set of the cover.
A finite selection of sets from the cover that still covers $E$.
An open cover that contains no finite collection of sets.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the open-cover definition of compactness?
options: Every open cover must already be finite.
Every finite collection of open sets must cover the set.
Every open cover can be reduced to finitely many covering sets.
Every compact set has no open covers.

questions.question: In the compactness definition, what must be true for every open cover of $E$?
options: It has no finite subcover of $E$.
It has a finite subcover of $E$.
It consists only of bounded sets.
It contains exactly one open set.

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$, which set is compact by the closed-and-bounded criterion?
options: $\mathbb{R}$

questions.question: In $\mathbb{R}$, why is $(0,1)$ not compact under the closed-and-bounded criterion?
options: It is not bounded.
It is not a subset of $\mathbb{R}$.
It has no open cover.
It is not closed.

questions.question: Which open-cover argument proves that $\{p,q\}$ is compact in a metric space?
options: One covering open set for $p$ and one for $q$.
Use every open set in the metric space.
Show that no open cover of $\{p,q\}$ exists.
Show that $p=q$ must hold.

questions.question: What does compactness guarantee about an arbitrary open cover of a compact set?
options: The cover must contain exactly one open set.
The cover must consist of compact sets.
The cover cannot have infinitely many members.
Finitely many members of the cover suffice.

questions.question: Let $X=[0,1]\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and let $f:X\to\mathbb{R}^k$ be continuous. What follows?
options: $f(X)$ is compact.
$f(X)$ is never compact.
$f(X)$ must be empty.
$X$ is not compact.
